section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from October 1941 concerning Japanese internal political developments, focusing on the fall of the third Konoye Cabinet and the establishment of the Tojo Cabinet. It contains diplomatic telegrams from Tokyo, Peiping, Shanghai, and Hankow reporting official policy statements, cabinet appointments, press commentary, and regional diplomacy regarding Thailand and the Soviet Union. The section also includes firsthand accounts of economic hardships and restrictions on foreign nationals in Japan, an address by former Foreign Service Officer Gregor C. Merrill analyzing Japanese militarism, and Military Intelligence Division analyses of the Japanese governmental system.

subfiles.about: Tail end of a confidential memorandum detailing living conditions, police surveillance, and difficult evacuation procedures for foreign nationals leaving Kobe in August 1941.
subfiles.from: A member of the staff of the National City Bank of New York
subfiles.summary: A returning bank employee's report describes postal censorship, surveillance of foreigners, travel restrictions, and strict evacuation procedures for the Tatsuta Maru's August 1941 Kobe departure.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan
subfiles.to: Boies C. Hart, Vice President, The National City Bank of New York

subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Hart's letter enclosing a memorandum on conditions in Japan prepared by a bank staff member.
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
keywords: National City Bank of New York
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks Hart for the National City Bank employee's Japan-conditions memo, noting it was studied carefully.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Boies C. Hart
subfiles.to: Boies C. Hart, Vice President, The National City Bank of New York

subfiles.about: Transmits to Ambassador Grew a copy of a confidential memorandum on Japanese conditions prepared by a National City Bank staff member.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State instructs Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, enclosing for his information a copy of the October 7, 1941 memorandum on conditions in Japan by a National City Bank employee. The enclosed memorandum discusses severe price controls, food and fuel rationing, ersatz clothing, currency and travel restrictions on foreigners, and the arduous embarkation of evacuees from Kobe on the Tatsuta Maru. The subfile also includes the State Department's internal record copy of the instruction.
subfiles.title: Department of State Instruction No. 2267 to the American Ambassador in Tokyo

subfiles.about: Reports the formal policy declaration and radio address of the newly inaugurated Tojo Cabinet, highlighting the omission of any reference to the Tripartite Pact.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the new Japanese government's declaration to settle China, build the Co-Prosperity Sphere, and strengthen defense; Tojo's address omitted the Tripartite Alliance, while Togo promised open diplomacy.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1656 from Tokyo regarding Policy Declaration of New Japanese Government

subfiles.about: Reports key administrative and ministerial appointments in the newly formed Tojo Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports key appointments: Suzuki to the Planning Board, Tani to Information, Hoshino as Chief Secretary, and Moriyama to the Legislature Bureau.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1655 from Tokyo regarding Cabinet Appointments

subfiles.about: Transmits Chinese intelligence on the Japanese Navy's war reluctance and the abrupt cancellation of an independent North China regime.
subfiles.summary: Butrick relays Chinese sources that Japan's Navy fears American/British fleets and resists risking war, expecting cautious Tojo policy, while a planned North China regime launch was called off by Sugiyama.
subfiles.title: Telegram 313 from Peiping regarding Japanese Navy Attitude and North China Developments

subfiles.about: Reports the appointment of Haruhiko Nishi as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs and analyzes its significance for Soviet-Japanese relations.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Nishi's appointment as Vice Foreign Minister, a Soviet-affairs specialist seen as trustworthy though not brilliant, pairing with Togo as another career diplomat not unfriendly to the Soviets.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1673 from Tokyo regarding Appointment of Haruhiko Nishi

subfiles.about: Assesses the resignation of the Konoye Cabinet and predicts an Army-led, pro-Axis successor government.
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Brigadier General, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.summary: Miles attributes the Konoye Cabinet's fall to Toyoda's failed U.S. economic-pressure relief, predicting a more Axis-leaning, Army-dominated successor exploiting any Soviet Siberian weakening.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Chief of Staff: Fall of the Japanese Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports inquiries by Japanese gendarmerie regarding American evacuation rumors and their assurances of peaceful local relations.
subfiles.summary: Spiker reports a Japanese gendarme asking if the consulate was evacuating after false German reports of an American conference, offering Army assistance for any future evacuation.
subfiles.title: Telegram 76 from Hankow regarding Japanese Gendarmerie Inquiries

subfiles.about: Refutes German news reports that the American Consul General in Shanghai called a conference to discuss the Japanese cabinet change.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart denies German reports of an emergency American meeting in Shanghai, confirming no such conference occurred.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1525 from Shanghai Denying Evacuation Conference Reports

subfiles.about: Summarizes editorials from major Tokyo newspapers on the formation of the Tojo Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes Tokyo press reactions to the Tojo Cabinet: papers see unchanged policy and hope for resolving the crisis, with one stressing readiness over war and another urging cabinet stability.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1654 from Tokyo regarding Japanese Press Reactions to Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: Summarizes press characterizations of Premier Tojo as a moderate and discussions of terms for Pacific peace.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Tokyo press viewing Tojo as a moderate army figure whose Togo appointment eases war fears, with papers urging the U.S. abandon Chiang and British alignment, or affirming friendly relations within existing policy limits.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1662 from Tokyo regarding Press Assessments of Tojo Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Reports British official views that the Tojo Cabinet favors armed action against the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: War Department bulletin reports British officials view the new Tokyo cabinet as pro-Soviet-action, calling the new Premier pro-Nazi and anti-Soviet, noting difficulty maintaining Moscow contacts.
subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Memorandum on British Official Opinion regarding New Japanese Cabinet
subfiles.to: Assistant Secretary of War, Assistant Chief of Staff WPD, State Department, and Director of Naval Intelligence

subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese press reporting on U.S.-Japanese negotiations, an air transport agreement with Portugal, and American naval statements.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits extensive Japanese press reports analyzing American reactions to the Tojo Cabinet, noting perceptions that Washington was adopting a more cautious and conciliatory tone toward Japan. The telegram reports the official text of an agreement signed in Lisbon establishing commercial air service between Palau and Dili in Portuguese Timor. It also discusses press denials of rumors that Ambassador Nomura or Counselor Iguchi would return from Washington, and notes Japanese press reactions to Secretary of the Navy Knox's speech warning of an unavoidable clash.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1689 from Tokyo regarding Press Coverage of U.S.-Japan Relations and Regional Developments

subfiles.about: Reports editorial enthusiasm in Tokyo newspapers for the convocation of an extraordinary session of the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes editorials on the November Diet session: Asahi cites new tax measures and political unification, while others see it as evidence of Tojo's constitutional respect and domestic rallying.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1688 from Tokyo regarding Convocation of Extraordinary Diet Session

subfiles.about: Reports press discussions on foreign policy themes for the Diet, Ambassador Tsubogami's interview with the Thai Premier, and criticism of U.S. economic warfare.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reviews press expectations that foreign relations, the German-Soviet war, and the crisis with Anglo-American powers will dominate the upcoming Diet session. A Domei dispatch details an interview between Japanese Ambassador Tsubogami and Thai Premier Phibunsongkhram, in which the Premier affirmed Thailand's strict neutrality and rejected rumors of a secret military pact with Britain. The telegram also summarizes a Nichi Nichi editorial warning that apparent American conciliatory gestures are superficial masks for economic warfare designed to deplete Japan's strength.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1691 (Sections One and Two) from Tokyo regarding Diet Session, Thai Neutrality, and U.S. Policy

subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of an address analyzing Japanese political mentality, bureaucratic pressure against Western interests, and imperial ambitions.
subfiles.summary: Former Foreign Service Officer Gregor C. Merrill transmits two copies of a speech delivered on October 21, 1941 to the Economic Round Table of San Francisco. Drawing on five years of diplomatic service in Japan, Merrill recounts personal experiences with police surveillance, bureaucratic harassment of foreign businesses, and the detention of Americans on espionage suspicions. He analyzes Japanese concepts of precedent, "face," and legal evasion, tracing how the February 26 Incident and the assassination of Finance Minister Takahashi empowered military extremists. Merrill warns that Japanese moderation is illusory, that Axis ties serve an unswerving ambition for Asian conquest, and that Japan will strike resource-rich territories when the opportunity arises.
subfiles.title: Letter from Gregor C. Merrill Transmitting Address to the Economic Round Table of San Francisco

subfiles.about: Transmits and highlights key sections of a comprehensive War Department intelligence study on the Japanese political and governmental system.
subfiles.summary: Alger Hiss submits a transmittal memorandum advising State Department officials to examine specific passages in an attached Military Intelligence Division study titled "Japan Political Estimate" dated August 20, 1941. The attached report opens with a detailed table of contents covering governmental organization, totalitarian trends, political factions, and foreign relations with various world powers. The opening pages analyze Japan's constitutional monarchy, the spiritual and political role of the Emperor under "Kodo" (the Imperial Way), political stability, the suppression of the Communist movement, and the complex balance of power between the Cabinet, the Imperial Household, and the military.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Military Intelligence Division "Japan Political Estimate"
subfiles.to: Adviser on Political Relations, Department of State
